notes:
I've written notes for vv. 25–48 below. The main gaps first: I didn't read Lutheran, Methodist, Pentecostal or Orthodox teachers on this passage, and I didn't find the netbible.org notes. Apart from one short Wesley quote, those traditions aren't covered. I found nothing on prosperity, word-of-faith or hyper-grace teaching about these verses, so that part is left out. Augustine's exposition was cut off before v. 25, so he only appears in passing. Verses with nothing found are left out (v. 35 is covered with v. 34).

**v. 25:** Keil & Delitzsch say "murmured in their tents" comes from Deuteronomy 1:27. The line looks back to the spies' report and the people's refusal to enter the land (Numbers 13–14). They count that refusal as Israel's fourth great sin in the psalm. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/106-33.htm

**v. 26:**
- **Meaning of the words:** Keil & Delitzsch explain "raised His hand" as a phrase for swearing an oath (Exodus 6:8; Deuteronomy 32:40). "Cast them down" picks up Numbers 14:29, 32. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/106-33.htm
- **A wording question (scholarly):** Keil & Delitzsch note that Ezekiel 20:23 is closely linked to this verse. Following the scholar Hitzig, they treat one Hebrew word in v. 27 as a copyist's slip: "to scatter" was written as "to cast down." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/106-33.htm

**v. 27:** Keil & Delitzsch say the threat of exile rests on the two great warning chapters, Leviticus 26 and Deuteronomy 28. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/106-33.htm

**v. 28:**
- **The setting:** Precept Austin places this in Numbers 25. On the way to Canaan, Midianite women drew Israel into idol worship, probably a fertility cult. https://www.preceptaustin.org/psalm-106-commentary
- **"Yoked":** The Hebrew word pictures two animals yoked together. Gill says Israel threw off God's easy yoke and put on an idol's. He calls it spiritual adultery. https://www.preceptaustin.org/psalm-106-commentary
- **Wesley (Methodist):** Wesley says Israel had fellowship with the dead god in the same way God's people have fellowship with God in worship. https://www.preceptaustin.org/psalm-106-commentary
- **"Sacrifices to the dead":** Most commentators take "the dead" to mean lifeless idols. The Treasury of Scripture Knowledge suggests the word means dead men, since pagan gods were often humans made into gods after death. Calvin stresses that the people feasted on these sacrifices. Spurgeon wonders whether they also joined in rites for contacting the dead. https://www.preceptaustin.org/psalm-106-commentary

**v. 30:**
- **What Phinehas did:** Barnes says Phinehas gave a leading offender immediate punishment (Numbers 25:7–8). https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/106-30.html
- **"Executed judgment" or "mediated"?** The Pulpit Commentary notes that some scholars (Kay, Cheyne) translate the verb as "mediated." https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/106-30.html
- **"Prayed":** Gill reports that the Targum (an ancient Aramaic paraphrase) and the Syriac version render it "he prayed." https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/psalms-106.html
- **"Made atonement":** The Greek Old Testament (Septuagint) reads "made atonement." https://www.blueletterbible.org/verse/kjv/psa/106/30/ Augustine's Latin text reads "appeased Him." https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801106.htm
- **Spurgeon:** Phinehas showed God still has champions in the worst times. Though a priest, he took on the task and showed no favouritism to the princely offenders. https://www.preceptaustin.org/psalm-106-commentary
- **Not a model for violence:** Guzik quotes John Trapp: this was an extraordinary prompting of God's Spirit and must not be copied. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-106/
- **Christ and intercession:** Bible Hub's study notes treat Phinehas as a picture of Christ, who intercedes for people. https://biblehub.com/study/psalms/106-30.htm

**v. 31: where Protestant traditions differ.** Does "credited as righteousness" mean justification?
- **Calvin (Reformed):** The verse raises a hard question, because Paul uses the same words about Abraham's faith. Calvin answers that God credits believers' works as righteous out of free grace, not because they earn it. Faith alone gives righteousness both to persons and to their works. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/106-31.html
- **Gill (Baptist):** This is not righteousness that justifies Phinehas before God. God approved the deed as a righteous act and rewarded it with a lasting priesthood. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/106-31.html
- **Jamieson-Fausset-Brown:** Here it was a single act, not faith in Christ, so it was not justifying righteousness. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/106-31.htm
- **Faith behind the act:** The Geneva Bible notes say the act showed his living faith, and he was accepted for his faith's sake. The Cambridge Bible calls it an act of faith that made Phinehas a true son of Abraham. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/106-31.htm
- **Precept Austin and MacArthur:** Precept Austin insists Phinehas was declared righteous on the basis of faith, not works. MacArthur calls it a rewardable act that showed faith, as with Abraham. https://www.preceptaustin.org/psalm-106-commentary
- **Spurgeon (Baptist):** His faith did the brave deed, and the deed became the evidence that he was righteous. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/spurgeon_charles/tod/ps106.cfm
- **Perowne (Anglican):** The verse has nothing to do with justification, although its wording fits James 2. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/106-30.html
- **Barnes (Presbyterian):** The deed proved he was a man who feared God. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/106-31.html
- **The priesthood:** The Pulpit Commentary notes that the "everlasting priesthood" of Numbers 25:13 has passed away, though the praise of Phinehas lasts. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/106-31.htm

**v. 32:** Constable places this at Meribah, where the people provoked Moses into striking the rock instead of speaking to it (Numbers 20:2–13). https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/106-33.html Henry says God then took Moses' leadership away from them just when they most needed it. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/106-33.html

**v. 33:**
- **Whose spirit?** Ellicott notes that the Septuagint and the Latin Vulgate say "his spirit," meaning Moses'. Hebrew usage, however, favours rebellion against God's Spirit. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/106-33.htm The Cambridge Bible calls Isaiah 63:10 decisive for God's Spirit. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/106-33.htm The Targum also reads it as God's Holy Spirit. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/106-33.html
- **Moses' fault:** Calvin says Moses was pushed by the people but was not blameless. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/106-33.html Barnes says Moses spoke as if everything depended on himself and Aaron. He adds that readers should not judge Moses harshly. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/106-33.htm
- **The Hebrew:** Clarke says the Hebrew means Moses "stuttered" with his lips, so carried away was he by anger. Guzik adds that God still held Moses responsible for how he reacted. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-106/
- **What his sin was:** Keil & Delitzsch call it impatience with a tinge of unbelief. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/106-33.htm Ellicott thinks the real problem was Moses briefly sharing the people's despair. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/106-33.htm
- **Catholic translation:** The Douay-Rheims renders the line "he distinguished with his lips." https://biblehub.com/par/psalms/106-33.htm

**vv. 34–35:** Keil & Delitzsch link this to God's repeated command, from Exodus 23:32 on, to remove Canaan's inhabitants. Because Israel didn't obey, the nations became a snare. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/106-37.htm Matthew Henry says sin runs downhill: leaving things undone opens the way to doing wrong. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/106-37.htm Henry also says Israel spared these nations out of a show of pity, but no one needs to be more merciful than God. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/106-47.html

**v. 36:** Gill traces a step-by-step slide: mixing with the nations, learning their ways, serving their idols, and finally sacrificing children. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/106-37.htm

**v. 37:**
- **The word for "demons":** Ellicott says it literally means "lords," that is, false gods. https://biblehub.com/psalms/106-37.htm Barnes says the word appears only here and in Deuteronomy 32:17. https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/bsb/psalms/106-37.html
- **Real evil spirits?** The Pulpit Commentary sees the Molech child sacrifices here. Against those who deny the word means evil spirits, it says it is hard to see what else it could mean. https://biblehub.com/psalms/106-37.htm The Cambridge Bible thinks the exact idea can't now be determined, perhaps "some kind of subordinate spirit." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/106-37.htm
- **Calvin:** Good intentions and zeal excuse nothing. The difference from Abraham offering Isaac was that Abraham acted in faith. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/106-37.html
- **Chuck Smith:** Behind idol worship stands Satan worship, and many idols were inhabited by demons. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/106-37.html
- **Piper (Baptist, Desiring God):** In a Sanctity of Life sermon, he applies vv. 37–39 to abortion. He also says this is not the psalm's main point. https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/they-poured-out-innocent-blood

**v. 38:** Keil & Delitzsch say the land was defiled by blood-guilt (Numbers 35:33). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/106-37.htm Henry says this made the holy land unfit to receive signs of God's favour. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/106-47.html

**v. 39:** Barnes says guilt drove them to worse crimes as they tried to make up for their sins. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/106-39.html Piper explains that Israel is pictured as God's wife, so idolatry is adultery, and in this extreme case prostitution. https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/they-poured-out-innocent-blood

**v. 40:** Henry says God took sin from His own people as more insulting than from outsiders. In "He abhorred His inheritance," the change was in them, not in God. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/106-47.html The Gospel Coalition's commentary describes God's reaction as both moral anger and disgust. https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/commentary/psalm-90-psalm-106/

**vv. 41–42:** The same TGC commentary says God carried out the punishment through "those who hated" Israel. https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/commentary/psalm-90-psalm-106/ The Bridgeway Bible Commentary ties vv. 40–46 to the cycle in Judges 2:11–23. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/106-47.html

**v. 43:** The TGC commentary calls this the turning-point line. It echoes Judges 2 and looks both back at the cycle of sin and forward to God's rescues. https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/commentary/psalm-90-psalm-106/ Keil & Delitzsch say Israel followed its own plans instead of God's, and so sank in its sins. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/106-37.htm

**vv. 44–45:** Henry says they were punished but not destroyed, "cast down, but not cast off." https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/106-47.html On God "relenting," Henry says God's unchanging mercy turns justice into mercy; no other change in God is meant. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/106-37.htm The TGC commentary takes the covenant to be the one with the patriarchs (Psalm 105). https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/commentary/psalm-90-psalm-106/

**v. 46:** The TGC commentary says God also used the nations to show mercy (1 Kings 8:50). https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/commentary/psalm-90-psalm-106/ Jamieson-Fausset-Brown say these signs of kindness encourage the prayer of v. 47. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/106-47.htm

**v. 47: when was the psalm written?**
- **During the exile:** Calvin and Barnes say the psalm was written while the people were scattered. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/106-47.html The Pulpit Commentary means Babylon specifically, where the scattering had stopped Israel's worship together. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/106-47.htm The TGC commentary sees a worship leader of the Babylonian exiles, around 560–540 BC. https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/commentary/psalm-90-psalm-106/
- **Possibly earlier:** Spurgeon points out that the verse appears in David's psalm in 1 Chronicles 16:35, which he thinks weakens the exile argument. He also reports Bishop Patrick's view that it means captives taken before David's time. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/spurgeon_charles/tod/ps106.cfm
- **Fulfilment:** Calvin sees the real gathering in Israel being grafted into Christ's body. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/106-47.html Bible Hub's study notes instead expect literal regathering in the land. https://biblehub.com/psalms/106-47.htm
- **A wider prayer:** The Pulpit Commentary notes the shift from "remember me" in v. 4 to "save us" here. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/106-47.htm The TGC commentary connects "gather us" with Psalm 107:3, the opening of Book 5. https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/commentary/psalm-90-psalm-106/

**v. 48:**
- **Part of the psalm?** Maclaren thinks this verse was probably added by an editor to close Book 4 of the Psalms. https://www.blueletterbible.org/comm/maclaren_alexander/the-expositors-bible/psalms-volume-three/psalm-one-hundred-six.cfm Jamieson-Fausset-Brown hold that it belongs to the psalm and also served to close the book. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfu/psalms-106.html
- **Worship use:** Henry says the people answering "Amen" and "Hallelujah" is a fitting way to join in public prayer and praise. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/106-47.html
- **Augustine:** He mentions the view that the five books of Psalms each end with "Amen." https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801106.htm
